data.text:
China doesn't need to build the best AI. It just needs to make sure you can't function without theirs. In Southeast Asia, that plan is already well underway.

A new report published April 23, 2026 by John Lee, Senior Fellow at the Hudson Institute, a Washington-based nonpartisan policy research organization, lays out Beijing's strategy in striking detail. The conclusion is uncomfortable: while the US is focused on winning the AI technology race, China is focused on winning the AI dependency race. And in Southeast Asia, China is currently ahead.

The strategy is deliberate and layered. Chinese firms, backed by state subsidies and cheap government loans, are flooding Southeast Asian markets with AI tools that are cheaper, faster to deploy, and immediately available, even if less advanced than American alternatives. The pitch is simple: don't wait years for a premium Western product. Take ours now.

The on-the-ground results are concrete. Alibaba Cloud has locked Indonesia's INDONET into a "channel partner" agreement, meaning INDONET now distributes Alibaba Cloud products and builds its own services on top of them. INDONET's future growth is now structurally tied to Alibaba. Chinese firm SenseTime has partnered with Malaysian company G3 Global to build a $1 billion AI industrial park. Huawei has embedded itself inside Indonesia's Bandung Institute of Technology, training the next generation of Indonesian engineers directly on Huawei systems. The students graduating from that program will build their careers around Chinese technology.

Then there's the surveillance angle. Most Southeast Asian governments have authoritarian characteristics. Chinese firms including Huawei, Hikvision, and Dahua have signed agreements with governments in Myanmar, Cambodia, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei to supply AI-enabled smart city and surveillance systems, the same tools Beijing uses to monitor its own population. For governments that want to track their citizens without Western human rights scrutiny, China is offering exactly what they need, no questions asked.

China is also flooding the region with open-source AI models, including DeepSeek, which are free to download and easy to adapt locally. While Western companies like OpenAI and Anthropic protect proprietary models to maintain their edge, Beijing is doing the opposite on purpose. Give the technology away, build dependency, then control the ecosystem those dependencies run on.

John Lee's report makes the broader point clearly. Southeast Asian nations are not naively falling for Chinese promises. They are making calculated hedging decisions, trying to extract maximum benefit from both sides without committing fully to either. The problem is that China's strategy is specifically designed to exploit that hedging instinct. Offer immediate benefits. Create infrastructure dependencies. Embed Chinese systems into local institutions. By the time a country realizes it is trapped, switching costs are prohibitive.

This is the same playbook China used to come to dominate global solar panel and electric vehicle supply chains. It did not start with better technology. It started with cheaper, faster, and more available. Market dominance came later, and with it, the ability to set standards, prices, and terms.

The countries most at risk right now are Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Brunei. All of them are desperate to catch up economically. All of them see AI as existential to their competitiveness. And all of them are being offered a shortcut by a country that understands exactly what it is doing.

The CCP is not selling AI to Southeast Asia. It is buying Southeast Asia's technological future, at a discount, while the window is still open.

While the US aims to become the global technological leader in AI, China has an industrial and commercial strategy to offer immediate benefits to Southeast Asian partners.

The US should not think about the AI contest in purely—or even primarily—technological terms. 

It is about presence, relevance, tailored solutions, and building ground-up local partnerships and networks. If the US fails to do better than China in these areas, it will lose the ability to shape the AI norms, standards, and practices in the region.
